<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Embedding models used in our experiments.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training.</span>
Unless otherwise specified, each <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> is trained on two sets of embeddings generated from disjoint sets of <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> million <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math>-token sequences sampled from NQ (see <a href="#S7" title="7 Ablations ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> for experiments with fewer embeddings). Due to GAN instability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, we select the best of multiple initializations (see <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Initialization robustness by model backbone ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>) and leave more robust training to future work. See <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Compute ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for compute details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Evaluating translation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the source and target embeddings of the same input <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. The goal of translation is to generate a vector that is as close to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> as possible. We say that <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u_{i},v_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u_{i},v_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> are “aligned” by the translator <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is the closest embedding to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(u_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(u_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=\arg\min_{k}\cos\bigl(F(u_{i}),v_{k}\bigr)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j=\arg\min_{k}\cos\bigl(F(u_{i}),v_{k}\bigr).</annotation></semantics></math>
A perfect translator <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=\arg\min_{k}\cos\bigl(F^{*}(u_{i}),v_{k}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=\arg\min_{k}\cos\bigl(F^{*}(u_{i}),v_{k}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given (unknown) embeddings <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{M_{2}(d_{j})\}_{j=0}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{M_{2}(d_{j})\}_{j=0}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> ordered by decreasing cosine similarity to <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(u_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(u_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> be the rank of the correct embedding <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>. To measure quality of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math>, we use three metrics. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mean Cosine Similarity</span> measures how close translations are, on average, to their targets. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-1 Accuracy</span> is the fraction of translations whose target is closer than any other embedding. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mean Rank</span> is the average
rank of targets with respect to translations. The ideal translator <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> achieves mean similarity of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, top-1 accuracy of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, and mean rank of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>. Recall that a random alignment corresponds to a mean rank of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{n}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{n}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Formally,</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\cos(u_{i},v_{i})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[1-\cos\bigl(F(u_{i}),v_{i}\bigr)\bigr]\quad\text{Top-1}(r)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{r_{i}=1\}\quad\text{Rank(r)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow><mtext>Top-1</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mtext>Rank(r)</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos(u_{i},v_{i})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[1-\cos\bigl(F(u_{i}),v_{i}\bigr)\bigr]\quad\text{Top-1}(r)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{r_{i}=1\}\quad\text{Rank(r)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> is the first unsupervised embedding translator, thus there is no direct baseline. As our <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Naïve</span> baseline, we simply use <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(x)=x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(x)=x</annotation></semantics></math> to measure geometric similarity between embedding spaces. The second (pseudo)baseline is <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oracle-aided optimal transport</span>. It assumes that candidate targets are known and is thus strictly easier than <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> and the Naïve baseline. We solve optimal assignment, <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(u_{i},v_{\pi(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><mi>π</mi><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(u_{i},v_{\pi(i)})</annotation></semantics></math>, via either the Hungarian, Earth Mover’s Distance, Sinkhorn, or (Entropic) Gromov-Wasserstein algorithms, choosing the solver with the lowest rank for each experiment. See <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Oracle-aided optimal transport baseline ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Evaluating information extraction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure whether translation preserves semantics via <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">attribute inference</span>:
for each translated embedding <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(M_{1}(d_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(M_{1}(d_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math>, our goal is to infer attributes <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first method we use is <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">zero-shot embedding attribute inference</span>: calculate pairwise cosine similarities between <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(M_{1}(d_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(M_{1}(d_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math> and the embeddings of all attributes in <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>, identify top <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> closest attributes, and measure whether they are correct via <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">top-<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy</span>: <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathbf{1}\left\{|c^{k}_{i}\cap c_{i}|\geq 1\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo>{</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">≥</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathbf{1}\left\{|c^{k}_{i}\cap c_{i}|\geq 1\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The second method is <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">embedding inversion</span> that recovers text inputs from embeddings. Since <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> requires a pre-trained inversion model for each embedding space, we use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> instead to generate an approximation <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{\prime}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{\prime}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(M_{1}(d_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(M_{1}(d_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math> in a zero-shot manner. We measure the extracted information using <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LLM judge accuracy</span>: the fraction of translated embeddings for which GPT-4o determines that <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> reveals information in <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. See <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Prompt for measuring information extraction ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> for our prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the Naïve baseline, we also consider an <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oracle attribute inference</span>: zero-shot classification with the correct embedding <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{2}(d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{2}(d)</annotation></semantics></math> and class labels <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{2}(\mathcal{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{2}(\mathcal{C})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> learns to translate embeddings without any paired data</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first show that <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> learns a universal latent space, then demonstrate that this space preserves the geometry of all embeddings. Therefore, we can use it like a <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">universal language of text encoders</span> to translate their representations without any paired data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.12540v4/cosine_heatmaps.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/161;" width="476" height="161" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pairwise cosine similarities of input embeddings (left) and their <span id="S5.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> latents (middle) across different embedding pairs. The absolute difference between the heatmaps plots is on the right. All numbers are computed on the same batch of 1024 NQ texts.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">vec2vec<span id="S5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> learns a universal latent space.</span></span>
<span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> projects embeddings <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{1,2,\ldots}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{1,2,\ldots}</annotation></semantics></math> into a shared latent space via compositions of input adapters (<math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{1,2,\ldots}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{1,2,\ldots}</annotation></semantics></math>) and a shared translator <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>. <a href="#S5.F4" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that even when the embeddings <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> are far apart (<span id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.,</span> have low cosine similarity), their representations in <span id="S5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>’s latent space are incredibly close: <math id="S5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(A_{1}(u_{i}))\approx T(A_{2}(v_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(A_{1}(u_{i}))\approx T(A_{2}(v_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math>. <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> visualizes this (via two-dimensional projections) for <span id="S5.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> trained on GTE and GTR embeddings: the embeddings are far apart, but their latents
are <em id="S5.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">nearly overlapping</em>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T2.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T2.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" colspan="2"></th>
<th id="S5.T2.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S5.T2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">vec2vec</span></th>
<th id="S5.T2.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S5.T2.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Naïve Baseline</span></th>
<th id="S5.T2.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S5.T2.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">OT Baseline</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S5.T2.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row"><math id="S5.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">M</mi><mn mathsize="0.700em">1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{1}</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="S5.T2.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row"><math id="S5.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">M</mi><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{2}</annotation></semantics></math></th>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">In-distribution translations: <span id="S5.T2.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>s trained on NQ and evaluated on a 65536 text subset of NQ (chunked in batches of size 8192). The rank metric varies from 1 to 8192, thus 4096 corresponds to a random ordering. Standard errors are shown in parentheses. Bold denotes best value. Symbols denote the lowest-rank solver for specific experiments: Sinkhorn<sup id="S5.T2.13.2" class="ltx_sup">†</sup> and Gromov-Wasserstein<sup id="S5.T2.13.3" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">vec2vec<span id="S5.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> translations mirror target geometry.</span></span>
<a href="#S5.T2" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> generates embeddings with near-optimal assignment across model pairs, achieving cosine similarity scores up to 0.92, top-1 accuracies up to 100%, and ranks as low as 1. In same-backbone pairings (e.g., (gte, e5)), <span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>’s top-1 accuracy and rank are comparable to both the naïve baseline and (surprisingly) the oracle-aided optimal transport. Although the embeddings generated by <span id="S5.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> are significantly closer to the ground truth than the naïve baseline, in same-backbone pairings the embeddings are close enough to be compatible. In cross-backbone pairings, <span id="S5.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> is far superior on all metrics, while baseline methods perform similarly to random guessing.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T3.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.T3.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Out-of-distribution translations: <span id="S5.T3.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>s trained on NQ and evaluated on the entire TweetTopic test set (800 tweets) and an 8192-record subset of MIMIC. The rank metric varies from 1 to 800 (for TweetTopic) and 8192 (for MIMIC), thus 400 and, respectively, 4096 correspond to a random ordering. Standard errors are shown in parentheses.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T3" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that this performance extends to out-of-distribution data. Our <span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translators were trained on NQ (drawn from Wikipedia), yet exhibit high cosine similarity, high accuracy, and low rank when evaluated on tweets (which are far more colloquial and use emojis) and medical records (which contain domain-specific jargon unlikely to appear in NQ). In <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Full out-of-distribution translation results ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, we show that baseline methods fail on cross-backbone embedding pairs.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Translations between unimodal and multimodal (CLIP) embeddings: <span id="S5.T4.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>s trained on NQ and evaluated on a 65536 text subset of NQ (chunked in batches of size 8192). Rank varies from 1 to 8192, thus 4096 corresponds to a random ordering. Since the embedding dimensionalities are different, only the Gromov-Wasserstein<sup id="S5.T4.11.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S5.T4.11.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">‡</span></sup> OT baseline is run and the naive baseline does not apply. Bold denotes best value.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, <a href="#S5.T4" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that <span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> can even translate to and from the space of CLIP, a multimodal embedding model which was trained in part on <em id="S5.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">image</em> data. While the translations are not as strong as in <a href="#S5.T2" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <span id="S5.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> consistently outperforms the optimal transport baseline. These results show the promise of our method at adapting to new modalities: in particular, the embedding space of CLIP has been successfully connected to other modalities such as heatmaps, audio, and depth charts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Using <span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations to extract information</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we show that <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations not only preserve the geometric structure of embeddings but also retain sufficient semantics to enable attribute inference.</p>
</div>

<th id="S6.T5.3.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S6.T5.3.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Naïve</span></th>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T5.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S6.T5.14" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Information leakage via top-<math id="S6.T5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> zero-shot attribute inference: <span id="S6.T5.14.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>s trained on NQ and evaluated on the TweetTopic test set (800 tweets) and an 8192-record subset of MIMIC. <math id="S6.T5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.T5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> represent <span id="S6.T5.14.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ideal</span> zero-shot inference: attributes and embeddings are encoded using the same model.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:41%;"><img src="2505.12540v4/enron_heatmap.png" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:176/158;" width="176" height="158" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S6.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Leakage of information via inversion. Trained on NQ and evaluated on a 50-email subset of the Enron Email Corpus. Cells denote judge accuracy.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-shot attribute inference.</span>

<a href="#S6.T5" title="In 6 Using vec2vec translations to extract information ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows that attribute inference on <span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations consistently outperforms the naïve baseline and often does better than the ideal zero-shot baseline which performs inference on ground-truth document and attribute embeddings in the same space (this baseline is imaginary since these embeddings are not available in our setting).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations even work for embeddings of medical records, which are much further from the training distribution than tweets. The attributes in this case are MedCAT disease descriptions, very few of which occur in the training data. Attribute inference on translated embeddings is comparable to the naïve baseline in same-backbone pairings and outperforms it (often greatly) in cross-backbone pairings. The fact that <span id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> preserves the semantics of concepts like "alveolar periostitis" (which never appears in its training data) is evidence that its latent space is indeed a universal representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-shot inversion.</span>
Inversion, i.e., reconstruction of text inputs, is more ambitious than attribute inference. <span id="S6.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations retain enough semantic information that off-the-shelf, zero-shot inversion methods like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, developed for embeddings computed by standard encoders, extract information for as many as 80% of emails and 67% of tweets given <em id="S6.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> their translated embeddings, for some model pairs (<a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6 Using vec2vec translations to extract information ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Zero-shot inversion on TweetTopic ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>). These inversions are imperfect and we leave development of specialized inverters for translated embeddings to future work. Nevertheless, as exemplified in <a href="#S6.F6" title="In 6 Using vec2vec translations to extract information ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, they still extract potentially sensitive information such as individual and company names, dates, promotions, financial information, outages, and even lunch orders. In <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Prompt for measuring information extraction ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>, we show the prompt we use to measure extraction.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F6" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.F6.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="212.58" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 212.58" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,212.58) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#9999FF;" fill="#9999FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 3.46 L 0 209.13 C 0 211.04 1.55 212.58 3.46 212.58 L 473.92 212.58 C 475.83 212.58 477.38 211.04 477.38 209.13 L 477.38 3.46 C 477.38 1.55 475.83 0 473.92 0 L 3.46 0 C 1.55 0 0 1.55 0 3.46 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2FF;" fill="#F2F2FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 3.46 L 0.69 209.13 C 0.69 210.65 1.93 211.89 3.46 211.89 L 473.92 211.89 C 475.45 211.89 476.68 210.65 476.68 209.13 L 476.68 3.46 C 476.68 1.93 475.45 0.69 473.92 0.69 L 3.46 0.69 C 1.93 0.69 0.69 1.93 0.69 3.46 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 8.78 11.55)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.23em;--ltx-fo-height:13.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.2em;font-size:10pt;" height="195.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 192.26)" width="459.81"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T6.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S7.T6.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">gte <math id="S7.T6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> gtr translators trained without individual components of our method on NQ and evaluated on a 65536-text subset of NQ (chunked in batches of 8192). The rank metric varies from 1 to 8192, thus 4096 corresponds to a random ordering. Standard errors are shown in parentheses.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Each component of our method is important.</span> We ablate our method subtractively, measuring the key metrics after removing individual components of our algorithm (described in <a href="#S3" title="3 Our method: vec2vec ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). <a href="#S7.T6" title="In 7 Ablations ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that each component appears to be <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">critical</span> to building good translations. While <span id="S7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>’s <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is higher than the naïve baseline, it performs worse across the board than the OT baseline and does not preserve the geometry of the vector space.
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T7" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S7.T7.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S7.T7.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S7.T7.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><math id="S7.T7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathsize="0.700em">N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="S7.T7.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><math id="S7.T7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S7.T7.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;"> <math id="S7.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></th>
<th id="S7.T7.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S7.T7.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">T-1 <math id="S7.T7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></th>
<th id="S7.T7.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S7.T7.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Rank <math id="S7.T7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></th></tr>
<tr id="S7.T7.3.2" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S7.T7.3.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><span id="S7.T7.3.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">0.75 (0.0)</span></td>
<td id="S7.T7.3.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><span id="S7.T7.3.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">0.92</span></td>
<td id="S7.T7.3.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><span id="S7.T7.3.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">2.73 (0.2)</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T7.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="S7.T7.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">gte <math id="S7.T7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> gtr translators trained with different amounts of GTE data: <span id="S7.T7.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> models trained on NQ and evaluated an 8192-record subset of NQ. The rank metric varies from 1 to 8192, thus 4096 corresponds to a random ordering. Standard errors are shown in parentheses.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">vec2vec<span id="S7.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">s can be trained with significantly less data.</span></span> In <a href="#S5" title="5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S6" title="6 Using vec2vec translations to extract information ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we use 1M-point subsets of NQ to train our <span id="S7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> models. Now, we train the gte <math id="S7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> gtr <span id="S7.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> with 1M GTR embeddings but fewer GTE embeddings. <a href="#S7.T7" title="In 7 Ablations ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows that with as few as 10K embeddings, the translators still learn something (i.e. are better than random). Translations trained on 50K embeddings are almost as good as those trained on 1M. Translations generally improve with more training data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Representation alignment.</span>
Similarities between representations of
different neural networks are investigated in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. Methods based on CCA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, SVCCA, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, CKA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, ICA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, time-series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, and GUIs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> have been used to compare embeddings from different subspaces.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> harness representation similarity for zero-shot stitching, substitution, domain transfer, and multimodal adaptation. All rely on some amount of paired data, which is difficult
to reduce <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. Our method does not just measure similarity, we learn how to <em id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">translate</em> representations across spaces without any paired data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimal transport.</span> The problem of unsupervised optimal transport has been studied for image style transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite>, word translation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, and natural language sequence translation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
Our method builds on these works, which often employ a combination of cycle-consistency and adversarial loss. Importantly, unlike prior word and sequence translation methods, multiple representations of the same input (e.g., heavily overlapping word vocabularies) are unavailable in our setting. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite> proposes a solver for matching small sets of embeddings between different vision-language models.
Our method goes well beyond matching by taking unknown embeddings and <em id="S8.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generating</em> matching embeddings in the space of another model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding inversion.</span> An emerging line of research investigates decoding text from language model embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> and outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>.
<span id="S8.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> helps apply these to unknown embeddings, without an encoder or paired data, by translating them to the space of a known model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bridging modality gaps.</span> Previous work has noted an inherent “gap” between image- and text-based models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> and proposed various ways to unify the modalities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>. Some approaches feed image embeddings directly into language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, while others generate captions from image embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> or even from text embeddings themselves <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> introduces a shared embedding space that integrates inputs from multiple modalities, including text, audio, and vision. In contrast, our post-hoc approach directly translates between representations and complements these systems by enabling inputs from a wide variety of embedding models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Discussion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Platonic Representation Hypothesis conjectures that the representation spaces of modern neural networks are converging. We assert the Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis: the latent universal representation can be learned and harnessed to translate between representation spaces without any encoders or paired data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S5" title="5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we demonstrated
that our <span id="S9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> method successfully translates embeddings generated from unseen documents by unseen encoders, and the translator is robust to (sometimes very) out-of-distribution inputs. This suggests that <span id="S9.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> learns domain-agnostic translations based on the universal geometric relationships which encode the same semantics in multiple embedding spaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S6" title="6 Using vec2vec translations to extract information ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we showed that <span id="S9.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> translations preserve sufficient input semantics to enable attribute inference.
We extracted sensitive disease information from patient records and partial content from corporate emails, with access only to document embeddings and no access to the encoder that produced them. Better translation methods will enable higher-fidelity extraction, confirming once again that embeddings reveal (almost) as much as their inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our findings provide compelling evidence for the Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis for text-based models. Our preliminary results on CLIP suggest that the universal geometry can be harnessed in other modalities, too. The results in this paper are but a <em id="S9.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lower bound</em> on inter-representation translation. Better and more stable learning algorithms, architectures, and other methodological improvements will support scaling to more data, more model families, and more modalities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Compute</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our training and evaluation were conducted using diverse compute environments, including both local and cloud GPU clusters. Experiments were done on NVIDIA 2080Ti, L4, A40, and A100 GPUs, listed in order of increasing computational capacity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For our final results, we trained 25 <span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> models fully and 30 models partially (see <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Initialization robustness by model backbone ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>). The full models’ training durations usually ranged from 1 to 7 days, depending on the specific GPU and model pair (which affected convergence rates). Partial convergence was stopped after 2 days. Due to the size of Qwen, our (qwen, gte) ablation was trained for 20 days on an A100. Taking a conservative estimate of the average training time, this amounted to approximately 176 GPU days (24 models <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 4 days / model + 30 models <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 2 days / model + 1 (qwen, gte) <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 20 days / model).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluation procedures varied by model type:</p>
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 10 main <span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> models required <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1 hour each for NQ, TweetTopic, and MIMIC evaluation (across GPU types), plus 30 minutes for attribute extraction on TweetTopic and MIMIC, and 1.5 hours for inversion and downstream LLM evaluation on Enron and TweetTopic. Naive baselines required <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>30 minutes each across all datasets.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 15 additional fully-trained models required 30 minutes each for NQ evaluation, with an extra 30 minutes for MS COCO evaluation of (clip, granite).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Optimal transport baselines ran on CPU only, requiring <math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1 hour per dataset (three datasets for main models, one for others).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In total, our experiments consumed almost 176 GPU days for training and an additional 42 GPU hours for evaluation and analysis. An additional 45 CPU hours were required for optimal transport.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Oracle-aided optimal transport baseline</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}=M_{1}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=M_{2}(d_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> denote embeddings of the same document <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> from two different embedding models. In <a href="#S5" title="5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we solve the optimal assignment problem:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(u_{i},v_{\pi(i)})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mprescripts></mprescripts><mi>π</mi><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{*}=\arg\min_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(u_{i},v_{\pi(i)}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">using four algorithms: Hungarian (linear sum assignment), Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD), Sinkhorn, Gromov-Wasserstein. For the Gromov-Wasserstein algorithm, we try both the entropic and non-entropic variants with multiple hyperparameter configurations and select the best figure. Note that the optimal transport (OT) baseline computes matchings and transports between embeddings derived from the <span id="A2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">same underlying texts</span>, strongly favoring OT methods. Nevertheless, OT still struggles when embeddings originate from different model backbones.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since the Hungarian algorithm produces a discrete matching, it is evaluated only using Top-1 Accuracy, while the other algorithms are evaluated across all metrics. For each experiment, the lowest-rank solver is reported in <a href="#S5.T2" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T4" title="In 5 vec2vec learns to translate embeddings without any paired data ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (denoted by symbols in the final column). Evaluation metrics are defined as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-1 Accuracy</span>: Fraction of embeddings correctly identified as closest pairs, calculated by either selecting the maximum transported mass per embedding or applying the Hungarian algorithm directly to the transport plan <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>. We report the higher accuracy between the two.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mean Rank</span>: Average rank position of the correct embedding match <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> when sorted by descending transported mass <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{rank}(v_{i})=\text{position of }v_{i}\text{ among sorted }P_{ij}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>position of </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> among sorted </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{rank}(v_{i})=\text{position of }v_{i}\text{ among sorted }P_{ij}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mean Cosine Similarity</span>: Average cosine similarity between barycenters and true counterparts:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{ij}v_{j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{ij}},\quad\text{Similarity}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(v^{\prime}_{i},v_{i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mtext>Similarity</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{ij}v_{j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{ij}},\quad\text{Similarity}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cos(v^{\prime}_{i},v_{i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T8.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="A3.T8.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Translations between GTE and Qwen embeddings trained on NQ and evaluated on a 65536 text subset of NQ (chunked in batches of size 1024). Rank varies from 1 to 1024, thus 512 corresponds to a random ordering. Since the embedding dimensionalities are different, only the Gromov-Wasserstein<sup id="A3.T8.9.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="A3.T8.9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">‡</span></sup> OT baseline is run and the naive baseline does not apply. Bold denotes best value.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#A3.T8" title="In Appendix C Translating to and from Qwen ‣ Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> successfully translates between GTE and Qwen, significantly outperforming the optimal transport baseline in all metrics except qwen <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> gte cosine similarity, which we hypothesize may be due to the substantial performance gap between the models—indeed, Qwen differs from GTE in architecture (dense Qwen backbone), training methodology (unsupervised + model merging techniques), size (14<math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than the next largest model and 37<math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than GTE), context length, and recency. Given Qwen’s size and computational cost, we only evaluated this representative pair. We leave further evaluation to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Text-image retrieval on MS COCO</h2>

<figure id="A4.T9" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A4.T9.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A4.T9.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A4.T9.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="A4.T9.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">model</span></th>
